              What MARVIN stands for

              MarsAdaptiveRoutingandVisualInformationNetwork

              One planner for a first human walk in Jezero Crater: it turns NASA orbital data and rover imagery into a route you can read, check and walk, in 3D and in VR.

              Take the project with you

              Source code, cached NASA data, panoramas, tests and project documentation in one ZIP. This download is refreshed with each published update. Copies already downloaded remain snapshots.

              Download project ZIP ↓

              Current published project snapshot

              THE CHALLENGE

              Make Mars data useful
              at human scale.

              Future Mars explorers need to connect scientific opportunity with terrain, travel limits, and a reliable return plan. NASA’s orbital maps and rover observations are distributed across separate archives, making it difficult to turn them into one local exploration plan.

              MARVIN brings those sources together in a mission-planning prototype for Jezero Crater. Choose a distance, time budget, and science objectives; explore historical surface panoramas; and generate a round-trip itinerary.

              THE MODEL WE TRAINED

              Terrain AI: reads Martian ground from rover photos

              We fine-tuned a SegFormer-B0 network (pretrained encoder from NVIDIA, our own trained weights) on NASA/JPL's AI4Mars labels, then exported it to ONNX. It runs in your browser, with no server, and labels each pixel of a Mastcam-Z panorama as loose ground or rock.

              –mIoU on AI4Mars held-out test
              –rock vs loose, our hand check on Jezero panoramas
              –4-class on the same check (we cut that)

              Where it shows up: the panorama overlay and a live in-browser scan; ground bars in Live views; a Terrain AI note in every route popup; the ground summary in CAPCOM's route brief; and CAPCOM's describe_terrain tool.

              What the planner actually calculates

              Routes follow a graph assembled from NASA’s historical Perseverance traverse. Nearby recorded vertices may be joined within 10 meters; these joins are explicitly identified in exported missions. Distances use a Mars radius of 3,396.19 km. Elevation profiles use recorded rover elevations, not a fabricated terrain surface. CAPCOM's lines are scripted from this data unless you connect the optional live-AI proxy.

              The planner greedily adds reachable science stops (or rewards new photographed locations when “More panoramic views” is selected) within both distance and time limits, including the return, experiment duration, and a 20% time reserve. It is a heuristic, not a guaranteed globally optimal solution. Science tasks are proposed activities, not claims that a particular mineral or biosignature exists at a stop.

              Terrain slope comes from a 20 m CTX DEM (Mangold et al. 2021): each route is checked against it and off-track spurs are slope-routed with an A* search. At 20 m per cell, rocks, sand stability, small cross-slopes, weather and suit constraints remain unmodeled. MOLA and THEMIS layers are regional context and should not be interpreted at individual-rock scale.

              Portable ESP32 companion

              Export a JSON mission with Mars coordinates, route points, science tasks, estimated timings and source attribution. This is a data interface for a future ESP32-S3 display. Hardware firmware, communication and real positioning are not implemented. Mars has no GPS constellation; the on-screen walk uses simulated position.

              Data credits & limitations

              Orbital imagery: NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona/USGS. Panoramas: NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU/MSSS. Traverse: NASA/JPL-Caltech Mars 2020 mapping service. Mars Trek, ODE and PDS provide access to the underlying archives.

              Detailed numeric DEM processing, mineral classification, weather time-series decoding and radar-profile interpretation require additional scientific ingestion. Their archives are available in Data archive; the app does not invent missing measurements. Panoramas use the last available rover waypoint at or before their capture sol, which is explicitly shown.

                Open this website directly in Meta Quest Browser on your headset. Choose a panorama or “Walk this route”, then select Enter VR and allow the immersive session.                 Stay in place: these are monoscopic historical photographs, not a walkable 3D reconstruction. The 360° image wraps around you; unphotographed sky and ground remain dark. Vertical framing is approximate.
